props.title: Only The Strong
props.initialSlug: Teacher uses capoeira to reach troubled students

sections.content: Only The Strong pioneered Capoeira in American action cinema, starring Mark Dacascos as Louis Stevens, an ex-Special Forces soldier teaching the Afro-Brazilian martial art to troubled high school students. The film follows the "inspirational teacher" blueprint of Dangerous Minds (1995) and Stand and Deliver (1988), but injects explosive martial arts sequences that showcase Capoeira's unique blend of dance, acrobatics, and combat. While mainstream martial arts films of the era like Kickboxer (1989) and American Ninja (1985) focused on karate and ninjutsu, Only The Strong brought Capoeira's dynamic movements to Western audiences.

sections.content: The early 1990s saw a surge in martial arts films incorporating lesser-known fighting styles. Rapid Fire (1992) showcased Brandon Lee's Jeet Kune Do, while The Quest (1996) featured various global combat styles. Only The Strong distinguished itself by focusing entirely on Capoeira's fluid movements and its cultural significance. Mark Dacascos, a skilled martial artist, spent months training in Capoeira to authentically portray the art form's distinctive techniques. SUBHEAD: Cultural Impact and Teaching Elements

Like Lean on Me (1989) and Dead Poets Society (1989), the film explores how an unconventional teacher can transform students' lives. But Only The Strong adds layers by incorporating Capoeira's history as a martial art developed by enslaved Africans in Brazil, disguised as dance to preserve their fighting traditions. The film's training sequences, set to traditional Capoeira music and featuring authentic movements, helped introduce Western audiences to this unique martial art form.
